hook: "These ads are crushing for our eCommerce clients right now:"
body: Antonioventre_ lists 9 ad formats currently crushing for his eCommerce clients: FaceTime call ads, customer service call, street interviews, trend ads, yapping ads, AI storytelling ads, founder story ads, podcast ads, and green screen reaction ads.
idea: Recorded-conversation ads — FaceTime calls and customer-service calls — are a distinct, high-performing creative category.
sequencing: Open with the authority claim: these are crushing for eCommerce clients.
Enumerate the 9 formats, leading with FaceTime call ads and customer service calls.
Attach a photo as implied proof.
The list itself is the content — no single format is dissected.
formatting: X text list with a photo attachment; agency-client results framing.
why_it_works: Conversation formats don't look like ads; viewers trust what they feel they are overhearing more than what is said to them directly.
what_to_steal: The two call formats for LC: founder calls a repeat customer about her stack, and recorded pre-purchase support calls answering waterproof/tarnish questions.

hook: "Call ads are quietly becoming their own category on Meta."
body: Antonioventre_ declares call ads their own category on Meta and names 4 working variations: FaceTime call ads (two people on a recorded video call), founder-customer calls (customer doesn't know it's coming, reaction recorded), customer service call ads (real pre-purchase questions answered one by one), and WhatsApp voice message ads (screen-recorded chat with voice notes). All work for one reason: a conversation doesn't look like an ad, and people trust what they feel they are overhearing.
idea: Every recorded-conversation variation works for the same reason — overheard trust beats addressed pitch.
sequencing: Declare the category: call ads are now their own thing on Meta.
Variation 1: FaceTime call ads — two people on a recorded video call talking about the product.
Variation 2: founder-customer calls — the founder calls a real customer who doesn't know it's coming; the reaction is recorded.
Variation 3: customer service call ads — real pre-purchase questions answered one by one.
Variation 4: WhatsApp voice message ads — screen-recorded chat with voice notes going back and forth.
Close with the unifying principle: overheard beats addressed.
formatting: X text list with a photo attachment.
why_it_works: Eavesdropping bypasses ad skepticism — the viewer feels like a witness to a real conversation, not the target of a pitch.
what_to_steal: The WhatsApp voice-note variation: screen-record a real LC customer voice note raving about her stack.

idea: Customer-call ads belong in the social-proof family — a recorded conversation is a testimonial that doesn't look like one.
sequencing: Headline promise: 30 scroll-stopping formats worth stealing.

hook: "An ad format that is going really crazy for us right now: the surprise customer call."
body: Antonioventre_ describes the surprise customer call format: the founder calls a real customer who doesn't know the call is coming, and it's recorded. The founder asks normal questions — why do you keep ordering, what changed since you started using it, would you recommend it. Nothing can be scripted; the customer's surprise is the whole ad. An ad-manager screenshot shows it as the top ROAS creative (4.80 on $20.9k spend) in a $112k set. It works because it's a testimonial that doesn't look like one.
idea: An unscripted surprise call from the founder to a real customer is an unfakeable testimonial.
sequencing: Name the format: the surprise customer call.
The setup: founder calls a real customer, the customer doesn't know it's coming, it's recorded.
The questions: why do you keep ordering, what changed, would you recommend it.
The rule: nothing scripted — the surprise is the whole ad.
The proof: top ROAS creative, 4.80 on $20.9k inside a $112k set.
The mechanism: a testimonial that doesn't look like one.
formatting: X text post with an ad-manager screenshot (photo) as proof.
why_it_works: Staged testimonials are legible as acting; a genuinely surprised person can't be faked, so the brain files it as evidence, not advertising.
what_to_steal: The 3-question script — 'why do you keep ordering / what changed / would you recommend' — filmed as a real surprise call to a 10-order LC customer.

body: William Kast distinguishes 2 types of creative diversity: production format vs creative framework. Example: pick UGC as the production format, then use it to make a day-in-the-life ad, a 3-reasons-why ad, an old-me/new-me ad, or a phone call ad. The matrix of formats × frameworks turns 1 winning message into 25 concepts — 'infinite winning ads'.
idea: Creative diversity comes from crossing production formats with frameworks — a phone-call ad is a framework any winning message can wear.
sequencing: State the distinction: production format vs creative framework.
Show most brands only use the production format (founder vs UGC vs static).
Give the example: UGC × day-in-the-life / 3-reasons / old-me-new-me / phone call.
Do the matrix math: formats × frameworks = 25 concepts.
Close with the payoff: infinite winning ads from 1 winning message.
formatting: X text post with a creative-diversity matrix image.
why_it_works: The matrix turns one proven message into dozens of fresh-looking ads, beating creative fatigue without needing new angles.
what_to_steal: Treat 'phone call' as a framework: take LC's winning waterproof message and reshoot it as founder-call, support-call, and voice-note versions.

hook: "We've been turning 1 winning ad into 5 with this framework."
body: William Kast's framework for turning 1 winning ad into 5: package the same winning message into different frameworks (day in the life, 3 reasons why, old me talking to new me, phone call ad) to reach different sub-audiences. Simply running different production formats is not creative diversity — the framework layer is what multiplies concepts.
idea: One winning message in five frameworks — including a phone-call version — beats five new messages.
sequencing: Claim: 1 winning ad becomes 5 with this framework.
The nuance: different production formats alone are NOT creative diversity.
Introduce the two layers: production format × creative framework.
List the example frameworks: DITL, 3 reasons, old-me/new-me, phone call.
Close with the payoff: the matrix multiplies one message into many ads.
formatting: X text post with a photo attachment.
why_it_works: Different frameworks reach different sub-audiences of the same persona while the proven message does the converting.
what_to_steal: The 1→5 repackaging playbook applied to LC's top waterproof angle, with the phone-call version as one of the five.

hook: "A call ad variation that is crushing for us right now: customer service call ads"
body: Antonioventre_ describes the customer-service call ad variation: instead of a testimonial praising the product, record a real pre-purchase support call where the customer asks the questions people actually ask before buying and support answers them one by one. Pull the questions from the real support inbox and comment sections, since viewers are stuck on the same 5-6 questions. It works because every unanswered question is a lost purchase — this format removes objections instead of piling on claims.
idea: A recorded customer-service call answering the 5–6 real pre-purchase questions is an objection-removal ad.
sequencing: Name the variation: customer service call ads.
The setup: a real pre-purchase conversation — the customer asks, support answers one by one.
Where the questions come from: the real support inbox and comment sections.
The contrast: most ads pile on claims; this one removes objections.
The payoff: the viewer hears their own doubt asked out loud and answered before ever reaching the product page.
formatting: X text post with a photo attachment.
why_it_works: The viewer hears their own unspoken doubt asked out loud and answered — objection-handling disguised as eavesdropping.
what_to_steal: Mine LC's support inbox for the 5–6 real questions (tarnish? waterproof? sizing? green skin?) and record one support call per question cluster.

hook: "The production rule that decides whether a testimonial-style ad works: the reaction cannot be scripted"
body: Antonioventre_ states the production rule for testimonial-style ads: the reaction cannot be scripted. The founder-customer call is the clearest version — the founder calls a real customer with no warning and asks why they keep ordering, how long they've used it, whether they see a difference. Scripting kills it; a slightly messy real reaction beats a perfect scripted one. Same rule for POV reaction ads: no face, product from the buyer's point of view, live unscripted reaction, minimal text and editing. Rawness is the mechanism, not a budget limitation.
idea: The unscripted reaction is the product — scripting a call ad destroys the exact mechanism that makes it convert.
sequencing: State the rule: the reaction cannot be scripted.
Give the clearest example: the founder-customer surprise call.
List the questions: why keep ordering, how long, do you see a difference.
State the corollary: the moment you script it, it dies.
Extend the rule to POV reaction ads: no face, buyer's POV, live reaction, minimal editing.
Reframe: rawness is what makes it work, not a budget limitation.
why_it_works: Humans are lie-detectors for staged reactions; messiness is the authenticity signal the brain trusts.
what_to_steal: LC's production rule: shoot call ads in one take, no re-takes, no teleprompter — publish the messy version.

hook: "We're seeing a tonne of trends on different visual formats outside of just AI."
body: Rahul Issar names 3 trends beyond AI: (1) greenscreen personal story with no product until late — the creator yaps an in-depth personal story, the viewer gets bought in, the brand lands later at high intent; (2) natives driving to a quiz funnel instead of PDP; (3) founder calling customers — not one-hit wonders, they continuously deliver bangers, and getting the founder on more ads shows behind-the-scenes of the brand.
idea: Founder-calling-customers is a durable, repeatable format — not a one-hit wonder but a system that keeps delivering.
sequencing: Trend 1: greenscreen personal story, no product until late — story earns attention, brand converts at high intent.
Trend 2: natives → quiz funnel, which builds purchase intent better than PDP for high-CTR creatives.
Trend 3: founder calling customers — repeatable bangers, plus behind-the-scenes brand access.
The takeaway: these are systems, not singles.
why_it_works: The format is a system (call any customer, anytime), not a single creative — so it compounds instead of fatiguing.
what_to_steal: Make it a recurring LC series: Jay calls a customer every week — the series itself becomes content and compounds.

hook: "Last week we tested a similar format: talking-head style where the creator calls a customer who just placed their 10th order."
body: Igor Woorts tested a talking-head format where the creator calls a customer who just placed her 10th order. The sequence was built to work as top-of-funnel: ask about problems → customer explains benefits and desired outcome → introduce the product last. They used the customer as the authority instead of a specialist or doctor. It's now the top spender in the client's campaign.
idea: A 10th-order customer is the ultimate authority figure — call her, let her explain the benefits, introduce the product last.
sequencing: The setup: creator calls a customer on her 10th order.
Make it TOF-safe: open on her problems, not the product.
The customer explains the benefits she experienced plus the desired outcome.
Introduce the product last.
The authority swap: the customer replaces the specialist/doctor.
The result: top spender in the client's campaign.
why_it_works: The 10th order is proof no doctor can match — loyalty is the credential — and the problem-first structure makes it top-of-funnel safe.
what_to_steal: LC's version: call a customer on her 10th order, open on her jewelry problem, let her sell the stack, product last.
